A ball’s fate depends only on the position it first occupies on the three-slot platform.

Success probabilities by starting position
1. Position 1 → ejected with probability 1⁄3.
2. Position 2 → 1⁄3 (instant win) + 2⁄3·(1⁄3) = 5⁄9.
3. Position 3 → 1⁄3 (instant win) + 1⁄3·(5⁄9) + 1⁄3·(1⁄3) = 17⁄27.

Thus Position 3 is best (≈0.6296).

Ball 3 is the only ball guaranteed to start in Position 3 (it is already there when play begins). All later balls reach Position 3 only with probability ≤0.6, giving them a lower overall chance of ejection.

Therefore, to maximize the probability of being the ball that gets ejected, you should choose ball number 3.
A ball’s chance of being ejected depends on the position in which it first appears on the three-slot platform.

Define states for a given ball:
A: in slot 3 B: in slot 2 C: in slot 1 D: ejected (win) E: rolls away (lose)

Transition probabilities per step (each piston fires with probability 1⁄3):
• From A: 1⁄3 → D, 1⁄3 → B, 1⁄3 → C
• From B: 1⁄3 → D, 2⁄3 → C
• From C: 1⁄3 → D, 2⁄3 → E

Let s_A,s_B,s_C be success probabilities from A,B,C.
  s_C = 1⁄3
  s_B = 1⁄3 + (2⁄3)s_C = 1⁄3 + 2⁄9 = 5⁄9
  s_A = 1⁄3 + (1⁄3)s_B + (1⁄3)s_C = 1⁄3 + 5⁄27 + 1⁄9 = 17⁄27 ≈ 0.63

Initial positions:
Ball 1 starts in C → success 1⁄3
Ball 2 starts in B → success 5⁄9
Ball 3 starts in A → success 17⁄27
Every later ball also first enters slot 3, so each has success 17⁄27.

Thus the highest attainable probability is 17⁄27, achieved by any ball that first appears in slot 3; the smallest-numbered such ball is 3.

If even one human were present, a vampire could not repeat the truthful statement "At least one of us is a human," because vampires always lie. Since every resident gives that same statement, there cannot be any mix of humans and vampires. Seeing a vampire earlier guarantees at least one vampire exists, so the only consistent scenario is that all 100 villagers are vampires.
Let H be the number of humans and V the number of vampires, with H + V = 100.

Everyone says the same sentence P: “At least one of us is a human.”

1. If both humans and vampires are present (H ≥ 1 and V ≥ 1):
   • P is true.
   • Humans (truth-tellers) could say P.
   • Vampires (liars) must say something false, so they cannot say P.
   Since everyone does say P, this mixed case is impossible.

2. If all 100 are humans (H = 100, V = 0):
   • P is true, and humans truthfully say it – logically consistent.
   • But you witnessed a vampire the previous night, so V ≠ 0.

3. If all 100 are vampires (H = 0, V = 100):
   • P is false (there are no humans).
   • Vampires must lie, so saying P (a false statement) is consistent.

Given the eyewitness proof that at least one vampire exists, only case 3 fits. Therefore every resident is a vampire.

Let the three boxes contain a,b,c coins with a≤b≤c and a+b+c=30.
Constraint (1) one pair differs by exactly 6 → either b=a+6, c=a+6 or c=b+6.
Enumerating all integer triples that satisfy these gives the only possible sorted distributions:
(0,6,24),(0,12,18),(1,7,22),(2,8,20),(2,11,17),(3,9,18),(4,10,16),(5,11,14),(6,9,15),(6,12,12),(7,10,13),(8,8,14).

Bob announces three guesses simultaneously; the host then permutes the boxes to minimise Bob’s gain.  If Bob’s guesses, put in non-increasing order g1≥g2≥g3, are matched with the coin counts in non-decreasing order a≤b≤c, Bob receives
R = (g1 if g1≤a else 0) + (g2 if g2≤b else 0) + (g3 if g3≤c else 0).

Take the host’s distribution (0,6,24). Whatever Bob chooses, the host can pair 0 with g1, 6 with g2 and 24 with g3.  Then Bob can earn at most g2+g3, with g2≤6 and g3≤g2, so R≤12. Hence no strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins.

Bob can attain this bound by guessing 12,12,12.  For every valid distribution at least one box holds 12 or more coins (because having all boxes ≤11 violates the total 30 and the 6-difference condition).  Thus he is certain to collect exactly one guess of 12 coins and may collect more, but never fewer than 12.

Therefore the largest guaranteed number of coins is 12, giving 12⋅1000 dollars.
Let the three guesses Bob writes on the boxes be g1≤g2≤g3.  
After seeing the guesses, the host may reorder the coin counts x1≤x2≤x3 among the boxes so that Bob’s largest guess is matched with the fewest coins, the second-largest with the second-fewest, and so on.  Bob therefore receives
R = g3·I(g3≤x1)+g2·I(g2≤x2)+g1·I(g1≤x3).

1.  If g1≥13 then the host can place (6,12,12):
   • 6<g3, 12<g2, 12<g1 ⇒ R=0.  
   So Bob must have g1≤12 to gain anything in the worst case.

2.  Suppose g1≤12.  The host can choose a distribution whose smallest two counts are both <g2 and whose largest count is ≥g1, for example
   (7,10,13)  (which satisfies the rules: 13−7=6 and totals 30).
   With x=(7,10,13) sorted against guesses g, the payoff is only g1, so the worst-case reward can never exceed g1≤12.
   Consequently no strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins.

3.  Bob can guarantee 12 coins by writing (12,12,12).  Whatever legal distribution the host picks, at least one box must contain ≥12 coins (because all three <12 would sum ≤33 yet cannot satisfy a 6-coin difference).  That box pays Bob 12 coins; the others may pay 0.  Thus the worst-case reward is exactly 12 coins.

Therefore the optimal strategy guarantees 12 coins, worth 12×$1,000 = $12,000.
